clue.text: Tune librarian composed that's played at the Proms

definitions.note: a phrase for a piece regularly performed at the Last Night of the Proms

indicators.note: music composed is put together, so the letters of the two words are arranged anew

explanation.surface: A librarian has written a tune that gets performed at the Proms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composed' looks like a musical verb, but it shuffles TUNE and LIBRARIAN together. The Proms is a London summer concert series whose last night always features this patriotic song.
explanation.definitionFit: This patriotic anthem is a fixture of the flag-waving Last Night concert, so it is a famous piece performed there.

clue.text: Casing from time arts flourished receiving study

indicators.note: one word receiving another takes it in, so the period's name holds the word for study

parts.note: the Renaissance was the era when European arts flourished
to con is an old verb meaning to study or learn

explanation.surface: Someone casing a joint draws on a historical period of artistic flourishing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Casing' looks like a covering, but it is slang for checking out a place before a crime.
explanation.definitionFit: Casing a place means scouting it in advance, and a scouting survey is a military-style inspection of ground.

clue.text: Left aboard Queen Elizabeth or similar

definitions.text: Left aboard Queen Elizabeth or similar

parts.note: being aboard is being in a vessel, giving IN
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, Queen Elizabeth

explanation.surface: Someone has been left behind on the famous ocean ship Queen Elizabeth or one like it.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: the pieces build the word, and the Queen Elizabeth is itself a great passenger ship.
explanation.definitionFit: The Queen Elizabeth is a famous Cunard ocean passenger ship, and others like it share the same general name for such vessels.

clue.text: Sweetener producing stroke on US medical drama

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece written on another sits below it, so the drama comes after the stroke

parts.note: a backhand is a stroke in tennis and similar games
ER is the American hospital television series

explanation.surface: A tennis stroke shown on a hospital TV drama makes for something sweet.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweetener is slang for a bribe, and a bribe passed discreetly is also called by this hyphenated slang term.

clue.text: Ape — one fellow captures it

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: one word capturing another holds it inside, so the fellow surrounds the word it

parts.note: a mate is a fellow or companion

explanation.surface: A man has caught an ape, as though at the zoo.
explanation.definitionFit: To ape someone is to copy their behaviour, a verb taken from monkeys mimicking people.

clue.text: Miss performing Hair following a cold

indicators.note: the hair word comes following the first two pieces, so it is written after them

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold on taps
a tress is a lock of hair

explanation.surface: A young woman is in the musical Hair after having caught a cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hair' looks like the title of the musical but just means a lock of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A miss is a young woman, and one performing on stage is a female player in a play or film.

clue.text: Sailors certainly not travelling round Venice originally

indicators.note: a word travelling round another encircles it, so the refusal surrounds the letter

parts.note: nay is an old word of refusal, meaning no

indicators.note: originally points to the first letter of Venice

explanation.surface: Sailors are refusing to go round Venice on their travels.
explanation.definitionFit: A country's sailors collectively form its sea force, the fleet and the people who man it.

clue.text: Where in the West End you can get luxury goods for free

definitions.text: Where in the West End you can get luxury goods
definitions.meaning: Liberty is a department store in London's West End selling luxury fabrics and goods; shopping there is being at that shop
free to act or go, not confined

explanation.surface: A puzzle about a place in London's West End where expensive goods are given away for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The West End is London's central shopping and theatre district, and Liberty is a famous upmarket store on Regent Street there.
explanation.definitionFit: Being free means not imprisoned or tied down, which this phrase expresses as an idiom.

clue.text: Cruelly avenging leader gets suspension from job

indicators.note: words treated cruelly are knocked about, so these letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A vengeful boss is punishing someone by suspending them from work.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain this phrase is the practice of paying an employee who is leaving to stay at home, away from the workplace, during their notice period.
explanation.definitionFit: This British idiom describes being kept away from work on full pay, a kind of paid suspension during notice.

clue.text: Criminal's touching screenplay — one's impressed

indicators.note: two pieces touching sit side by side with nothing between

parts.note: a con is a convict, a criminal; the 's is a link
a film's screenplay is its script

explanation.surface: A crook is moved by a touching film script, as if one were impressed by it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'touching' and 'impressed' pose as emotional words; to impress also once meant to force men into service.
explanation.definitionFit: To impress is an old term for forcing someone into military service, so one so forced is a drafted recruit.

clue.text: Rogue that's shunned in football club

indicators.note: a word shunned is kept away, so the little word in is dropped from the rogue

parts.note: a villain is a rogue or scoundrel

explanation.surface: A rogue is not welcome in a football club.
explanation.walkthrough: The club is Aston Villa of Birmingham, usually called just by its short name.
explanation.definitionFit: Aston Villa is an English football team, commonly known by the second word of its name alone.

clue.text: What may be dummy run, not hard to go round

indicators.note: one word going round another encloses it, so the word not wraps the letter for run

parts.note: R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for a run
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A trial run for something meant to be easy turns out not to be hard to get around.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge, one partner's hand is laid face up as the dummy, and the compass positions name the four players; this seat is often the dummy in printed problems.
explanation.definitionFit: In bridge diagrams the compass seats name the players, and this seat is frequently the dummy hand laid face up.

clue.text: State linking Indiana with Vermont

indicators.note: the closing letter is joined with the start of the next state name
the link between two state names written side by side is where one ends, its final letter

parts.note: the opening letters of the state name, where it touches the one before

explanation.surface: A US state forms a link between Indiana and Vermont.
explanation.walkthrough: Write the two names together and the letters linking them run across the join: the end of Indiana and the start of Vermont. 'State' pretends to be a US state but is a verb meaning declare.
explanation.definitionFit: To state something is to declare it firmly, the same as asserting it.

clue.text: President, Democrat, lying

parts.note: Abe is Abraham Lincoln, the US President
D is the abbreviation for a Democrat in US politics

explanation.surface: A President and a Democrat are accused of not telling the truth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lying' looks like telling untruths but means lying down.
explanation.definitionFit: Lying down in the sense of resting horizontally, especially in one's bed, is what this old word means.

clue.text: Poison that could have done for Lebanon lad

indicators.note: something done for is ruined or wrecked, so the letters are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A poison that might have killed a young man from Lebanon.
explanation.definitionFit: Deadly nightshade is a highly toxic plant, and its extract is a well-known poison.

clue.text: An Italian poet that's rather slow

parts.note: Dante Alighieri is the great Italian poet of the Divine Comedy

explanation.surface: An Italian poet is described as being a little dim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rather slow' suggests dim-witted, but it is the musical tempo marking, slower than moderate.
explanation.definitionFit: This musical tempo marking means at a moderately slow, walking pace.

clue.text: Sideline a team that's secured draw

indicators.note: letters secured by the words are held inside them, run across the phrase

explanation.surface: A manager benches a team that has managed to get a draw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'draw' looks like a football result but is the verb to sketch.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw a shape is to sketch or trace its outline precisely.

clue.text: You and I beset by noxious gas put in office

indicators.note: a word beset by another is surrounded by it, so the gas wraps the pronoun

parts.note: sarin is a toxic nerve gas
you and I together are we

explanation.surface: A couple are surrounded by a poisonous gas in a workplace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'office' looks like a workplace but means an official post.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting someone in office means formally installing them with an oath at the start of their term.

clue.text: What you do with holy books having resources

parts.note: what you do with this crossword clue is work it out
NT is the New Testament, a collection of holy books

explanation.surface: A question about what one should do with sacred scriptures.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue speaks to the solver: what you do with a crossword is crack it.
explanation.definitionFit: A company or person able to pay their debts is said to be financially sound, having enough money.

clue.text: Laugh about Western platform for pithy comments

indicators.note: one word about another surrounds it, so the laugh goes round the letter

parts.note: a titter is a nervous little laugh

explanation.surface: Someone laughs at a western-themed site for short remarks.
explanation.definitionFit: The social media service, now renamed X, limited posts to short messages, making it a stage for brief quips.

clue.text: Mother to place bet with an Asian

parts.note: ma is a familiar word for mother
to lay a bet is to place one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A mother goes to bet with someone from Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from Malaya, the peninsula now part of Malaysia, is a person from Asia.

clue.text: Official's providing prime minister with test

definitions.note: a possessive noun standing for an adjective meaning belonging to a civic official

parts.note: Theresa May was a British prime minister
an oral is a spoken examination

explanation.surface: A prime minister is set a test by an official.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes what belongs to a town's elected chief civic official, as an official's chain or duties.

clue.text: Relation making visit 'abitually

indicators.note: the dropped opening H in the clue word shows the H being dropped from the verb too

parts.note: to haunt a place is to visit it habitually

explanation.surface: A relative calls round regularly, said in a Cockney accent.
explanation.walkthrough: To haunt a place is to visit it habitually; written without its H, as 'abitually is, it gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A parent's sister is a family member, one kind of relative.

clue.text: Very small container with unknown quantity

parts.note: a tin is a metal container
Y is an algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: A very small container holds an amount nobody knows.
explanation.definitionFit: Something very small is minute, the adjective a near synonym meaning minuscule.

clue.text: Clubs toured by twin related to an aristocrat

indicators.note: something toured by another is gone around, so the twin word circles the letter

parts.note: dual means double or twin
C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs

explanation.surface: Clubs visited by twins with noble connections.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective refers to a duke, a high-ranking noble, as in a duke's palace.

clue.text: Make friends with Prince Charlie

parts.note: to chum up is to make friends

explanation.surface: Someone is told to befriend Prince Charlie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie' looks like the prince's name but is British slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A charlie is British slang for a fool, and this word is another term for a silly person.

clue.text: Pray to circumvent river hazard when sailing

indicators.note: to circumvent is literally to go around, so the plea encloses the letter

parts.note: to pray someone is to beg them
R is the map abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Sailors pray to get around a dangerous river.
explanation.definitionFit: An iceberg drifting in the sea is a danger to ships, and this short word names one.

clue.text: Irritate husband in restaurant

indicators.note: the husband's letter is placed in the eatery's name

parts.note: a cafe is a small restaurant

explanation.surface: A husband becomes annoying when out at a restaurant.
explanation.definitionFit: To irritate can mean to rub sore, and also to annoy, both senses of this verb.

clue.text: What's natural at spinning

indicators.note: letters set spinning are tumbled around into a new order

explanation.surface: A question asks what creature is naturally gifted at spinning.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition as well: this large hairy spider is naturally good at spinning silk.
explanation.definitionFit: A spider spins silk by instinct, and this large hairy one is a famous example.

clue.text: Writer on crime's done paralegal working

indicators.note: letters set working are put into new arrangement, as if in operation

explanation.surface: A crime writer's work has been done by a paralegal.
explanation.definitionFit: The American author wrote early detective stories such as The Murders in the Rue Morgue, so he wrote about crime.
